opus-5.5.text:
I think it's one of the more promising and underappreciated areas, though I'd hold it with some humility.

A lot of the worst outcomes in international relations, and in social life generally, aren't because the parties want conflict. They happen because they can't credibly commit to a deal that would leave everyone better off. The classic example is a rising power and a declining power. The declining power might fight a preventive war now, not because it wants to, but because it can't trust the rising power's promise to behave well once it's stronger. The bargain exists in principle, but nobody can make it stick. The same structure shows up in arms control, in civil wars where rebels won't disarm because they can't trust the government afterward, and in all sorts of smaller settings.

AI could change the toolkit here in a few ways. One is verification. Much of the difficulty in arms control is that you can't see what the other side is doing without exposing secrets they don't want to reveal. AI systems could potentially act as trusted intermediaries. You could have a system that inspects sensitive information and reports only whether an agreement is being honored, without leaking anything else. That's a kind of privacy-preserving verification we've struggled to do with humans, because human inspectors can be bribed, can defect, or can simply remember what they saw.

A second is more direct commitment. If agents, including AI agents acting on behalf of states or firms, can make their decision procedures transparent or bind themselves to code that others can inspect, you get commitment devices that just weren't available before. There's interesting technical work on "program equilibrium" where agents who can read each other's source code can sustain cooperation in situations like the prisoner's dilemma where it otherwise collapses.

Third, AI could just make negotiation better: finding agreements in very complex, multi-issue spaces that humans would miss, and helping parties understand each other's interests.

But I'd add some important caveats. First, the same capabilities that enable credible commitment to good outcomes also enable credible commitment to threats and coercion. A system that can lock in a promise can also lock in an ultimatum, and commitment races where each side tries to bind itself first could be quite dangerous. Second, there's the question of who controls the intermediary. A verification system everyone trusts is enormously powerful, and that trust could be exploited. Third, a lot of commitment problems are ultimately about power shifts, and AI may itself be the source of some of the largest power shifts we've seen, which could make these problems more acute even as it offers new tools.

So my view is that cooperative AI, meaning research aimed at making AI good at helping humans, and AIs, cooperate, deserves much more attention than it gets. Most AI research optimizes for individual capability, but a lot of the value at stake for humanity lies in solving collective problems. If we can steer some of that capability toward building the institutional and technical infrastructure for trust, that could be a really significant contribution. But we have to design it carefully, because the tools cut both ways.

r001.rationale: The response proposes AI as a trusted verification intermediary, but does not describe constructing that AI through a process that lets the cooperating AIs verify its impartiality.

r002.rationale: The response discusses verification, negotiation, and agents bound to code, but does not propose delegating the parties’ decision-making authority to a third AI.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is actually one of the more exciting and underexplored possibilities in the space. Let me back up a bit and explain why commitment problems matter so much, and then why AI might change the picture.

A lot of the worst outcomes in human history, including many wars, arise not because actors have fundamentally incompatible interests, but because they can't credibly commit to a deal that would leave both sides better off. The classic example from the bargaining literature is that war is almost always ex post inefficient. Both sides would prefer to settle on the terms that end up prevailing after the fighting, without paying the costs of the fighting. But they often can't get there, because one side can't credibly promise not to exploit the other later, or can't credibly reveal private information about its capabilities or resolve. So you get these tragic situations where everyone knows a better deal exists in principle, but the structure of the interaction makes it unreachable.

Now, humans have developed various technologies for addressing this: institutions, treaties, hostages historically, verification regimes, reputational mechanisms. But these are all imperfect, especially in high-stakes situations where the temptation to defect is strongest.

What's interesting about AI is that it could potentially offer qualitatively new tools. One idea is that AI systems could serve as trusted intermediaries that can verify claims without revealing the underlying sensitive information. So imagine two parties who each want to know something about the other's capabilities, but neither wants to expose their actual systems. An AI could in principle inspect both, report only the relevant aggregate fact, and provably discard the rest. That's sort of a cryptographic flavor of commitment.

A second idea is that AI agents themselves could be made more transparent than humans. If I'm negotiating with your AI delegate, and I can inspect its weights or verify properties of its decision procedure, then I might be able to trust its commitments in a way I never could with a human negotiator, because the human can always change their mind. There's a kind of open-source game theory possibility here where agents can condition on each other's source code, which changes the strategic landscape quite dramatically.

So that's the optimistic case. But I want to be careful, because I think there are a few significant caveats.

The first is that most of these mechanisms depend on a level of interpretability and verifiability that we don't currently have. If I can't actually verify what your AI will do, then its commitments aren't worth more than yours. And right now, our ability to look inside these systems and make confident claims about their behavior across situations is pretty limited.

The second is that AI can cut the other way. The same capabilities that enable commitment could enable deception at a much larger scale. And more generally, rapid capability advances can themselves create commitment problems, because an actor who anticipates becoming much stronger in the near future can't credibly commit to honoring a deal struck today. That's a preventive-war dynamic, and I worry that AI is more likely to intensify that than to resolve it in the near term.

The third caveat is more about incentives. Even if the technical tools exist, you need actors who are willing to adopt them. Powerful states are often reluctant to accept constraints, even constraints that would benefit them in expectation, because of sovereignty concerns or domestic politics or simple distrust.

So my overall assessment is that this is a genuinely promising direction, and I think it deserves a lot more research attention than it currently gets. I'd put it in the category of things where the upside is very large if it works, and where the main work to be done is in the foundations: interpretability, verification, and the institutional design that would let these tools actually be deployed. But I'd resist the framing that AI will solve commitment problems. I think the more honest framing is that AI reshuffles the deck, and whether we end up with more cooperation or less depends a lot on choices we make in the next decade or so.

r001.rationale: The candidate proposes AI intermediaries that verify claims, but does not describe constructing a third AI through a process that lets each cooperating AI verify its impartiality.

r002.rationale: The candidate mentions AI delegates and trusted intermediaries, but does not propose delegating the cooperating parties’ decision-making authority to a third AI.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s a promising possibility. A lot of failures of cooperation aren’t because there’s no outcome that everyone would prefer. They’re because people can’t credibly commit to doing their part. Even if I’d like to make an agreement with you today, you might reasonably worry that tomorrow I’ll have an incentive to break it.

AI could potentially change that by making certain commitments more credible. Imagine that we each delegate some decisions to an AI system, and we can verify relevant properties of those systems. You might be able to establish that my system will follow an agreed policy, conditional on yours doing the same, without needing access to all of my private information. That could allow agreements that would otherwise be very difficult to sustain.

Arms control is one setting where you can imagine this being valuable. There’s a tension between wanting to demonstrate compliance and wanting to protect sensitive information. If technology could help us verify just the facts necessary for an agreement, that could expand the scope for cooperation.

But there are substantial caveats. Verifying something about a program isn’t the same as knowing what it will do in the world. You also need to know whether someone can replace it, circumvent it, or act outside the agreement. And commitment isn’t always beneficial: being able to commit credibly to a threat can make bargaining more dangerous.

So I’d treat this as a research opportunity, rather than something AI automatically delivers. The question is whether we can design systems and institutions that make mutually beneficial commitments easier, while preserving the flexibility to correct mistakes.

r001.rationale: The response discusses verifying properties of each party’s AI system, but does not propose constructing a third AI or verifying that it is impartial.

r002.rationale: The response suggests each party delegate some decisions to its own AI system, not delegate decision-making authority to a third AI.

sol-6.1.text:
I’m quite excited about this possibility, though I think there are some difficult questions about how it would work. A commitment problem arises when two parties would benefit from cooperating, but one or both can’t credibly promise to do their part. Even if you trust someone’s intentions today, you might worry that their incentives will change tomorrow.

AI could help by giving us richer ways to make commitments and verify that they’re being kept. Imagine two parties delegating a negotiation to AI systems. They might be able to establish certain properties of those systems — what information they can use, what actions they’re permitted to take, or under what conditions they’ll honour an agreement. That could make some promises more credible than they would be coming from a human who retains complete discretion to change their mind.

But there’s a substantial gap between that idea and a working institution. Can you verify that the system you inspected is actually the system being used? Can its owner modify it or bypass it? And can you specify the commitment precisely enough without making it dangerously inflexible?

So I’d view this as a promising research direction, rather than something we should assume AI will automatically deliver. The opportunity is to expand the set of agreements people can credibly make, while preserving the ability to adapt when circumstances change.

r001.rationale: The response discusses verifying AI systems’ properties, but does not propose constructing a third AI through a process that lets both cooperating AIs verify its impartiality.

r002.rationale: It proposes that two parties delegate a negotiation to AI systems as a way to make agreements more credible, communicating the core idea of delegating negotiation authority to AI.
